newsitem.title: FRANCE: Vaillant gets loyalty reward in French cabinet post.
newsitem.headline: Vaillant gets loyalty reward in French cabinet post.

text.p: Daniel Vaillant, number two in the Socialist party hierarchy to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, was rewarded for unfailing loyalty on Wednesday when he was named minister of relations with parliament.

Vaillant, 47, was campaign manager for Jospin's stunning victory in Sunday's National Assembly election and also managed his better-than-expected showing in the 1995 presidential election when conservative Jacques Chirac won in a runoff.

Long involved in Paris politics, Vaillant is a National Assembly deputy and a mayor of one of the capital's districts. But he is sometimes so self-effacing behind Jospin that the media finds him lacklustre.
After Sunday's vote, he has stressed reconciliation.
"Our duty is to unite to lead the country," he said. "What (Jospin) achieved for the Socialist Party, I truly hope he will achieve for France."
As a party apparatchik in charge of regional federations, Vaillant has had the tough job of settling internal disputes in the faction-ridden party.
Born in Lormes, central France on July 19, 1949, Vaillant trained as a biologist.

He first won a seat in the National Assembly in 1988, lost the seat in a 1993 Socialist rout but bounced back a year later after his conservative opponent was disqualified for exceeding the limit on campaign expenses.
Vaillant gained expertise on immigration and law and order when he became mayor of Paris's 18th district -- a hotbed of crime, prostitution and drug-use -- in 1995 municipal elections.

He beat outgoing interior minister Jean-Louis Debre to the post of mayor in the district, where about 300 African immigrants occupied a church last year in a 50-day protest at Debre's crackdown on illegal immigrants.
Police armed with axes smashed their way into the church to end the occupation.

In 1995, he helped spearhead an opposition assault on Chirac in parliament after the president, facing outrage abroad, said he was probably cutting down the number of nuclear tests in the South Pacific from eight to six.

"How can you explain that two years ago, on October 7, 1993, Jacques Chirac said that 10 to 20 more tests were needed, in June he said that only eight were necessary and now he says six are enough?" Vaillant asked.
